newsitem.title: JORDAN: Chirac, Hussein worried over Mideast peace outlook.
newsitem.headline: Chirac, Hussein worried over Mideast peace outlook.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac and Jordan's King Hussein say they are concerned about the faltering Middle East peace process.

Chirac arrived in Jordan on Wednesday from the Palestinian territories where he received a hero's welcome after a tense two days in Israel, where his visit was marred by heavy security, diplomatic incidents, media hostility and public indifference.

After a first private session with the king, a spokesman quoted Chirac as saying: "I informed him of a certain worry which I have. We share the same feeling about the evolution of the region and the peace process. We share the same anxiety."
King Hussein struck a similar note of concern, warning in a dinner toast: "The only alternative to peace in our region is the end of all hope and an accelerated slide towards the abyss."

Chirac reported to the Jordanian monarch on his talks with Syrian, Israeli and Palestinian leaders on a Middle East tour aimed at increasing French and European political influence on stalled Arab-Israeli peace negotiations.

At a joint news conference with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat earlier in the day in Ramallah, Chirac said the U.S.-driven peace process appeared to have run out of steam and the Europeans could help inject a vital element of confidence.

Hours after he left the Gaza Strip, Israel imposed a total closure of the Palestinian territories in what it said was a measure to prevent possible attacks on the anniversary of the assassination of Palestinian Islamic Jihad leader Fathi Shqaqi in Malta by suspected Israeli agents.
King Hussein said the people of the Middle East looked for "an active and supportive European role" to help build peace on solid, sustainable foundations.
He made no mention of the Palestinians in his dinner speech.

In contrast to Chirac's vibrant plea in Israel and Ramallah for a Palestinian state, King Hussein told the French leader only that the Palestinians must have the right to live on their own soil, according to the French spokesman.
Jordan ruled the West Bank until the 1967 Middle East War, when Israel captured the area and the Jordanian-held eastern sector of Jerusalem.

Chirac used his dinner speech to appeal for international action to ease the plight of the civilian population of Iraq. He noted that the U.N. embargo on Iraq, imposed after President Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in 1990, continued to harm the economy of neighbouring Jordan.
"I hope that once it has fulfilled all the obligations set by the U.N. Security Council, that great country can return to its rightful place in the community of nations," said Chirac.
"But as of now, however, we must prevent the humanitarian plight of the Iraqi people from getting worse. This is why France advocates the rapid implementation of Resolution 986."

That resolution would enable Baghdad to sell limited amounts of oil to buy food and medicines. A deal to implement the policy, struck in May, has been blocked by the United States since a clash with Iraq in September over Baghdad's intervention in fighting between rival Kurdish factions in northern Iraq.

Chirac is due to address the Jordanian parliament on Thursday. France is expected to sign an agreement to upgrade Jordan's ageing Mirage III fighters and to provide soft loans and grants totalling up to 100 million francs ($20 million).
Chirac flies to Lebanon on Thursday afternoon.
